title: VPC Peering and Interconnect Design Playbook for Enterprise Private Deploys
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents recommended network topology patterns, routing policies, provisioning steps, validation checks, and operational runbooks for establishing VPC peering, carrier interconnects (Direct Connect / Interconnect), and encrypted transit for Redwood private deployments. It is intended for platform engineers, solutions engineers, and SREs executing enterprise VPC/private control-plane integration work.

Scope: covers cloud VPC peering, dedicated interconnects, transit gateways/hubs, VPN fallback, peering security controls, MTU and path MTU discovery guidance, route propagation and filtering, Terraform examples, acceptance test suites, and day‑2 runbook actions for failover, maintenance, and rollback. Does not cover vendor-specific switch fabric design beyond customer edge considerations.

Key goals
- Provide deterministic latency and predictable bandwidth to the private control plane.
- Ensure isolation between customer data plane and Redwood management/control traffic where required.
- Provide clear rollback and fallback steps that do not require on‑site access.
- Standardize verification and telemetry collection for troubleshooting and billing reconciliation.

High-level topologies (choose one per customer depending on security and SLA)

1) Direct Interconnect + Transit Gateway (Recommended for enterprise)
- Customer uses a carrier or cloud provider direct interconnect (e.g., AWS Direct Connect, GCP Dedicated Interconnect).
- Interconnect terminates at a transit gateway or cloud router in a dedicated backbone account/tenant.
- Transit routes select between private control plane subnets and customer application subnets using route tables and VRFs.
- BGP sessions advertise only approved prefixes; route filtering enforced on both sides.

2) VPC Peering (SMB / Non-sensitive)
- Peer point-to-point between customer VPC and Redwood-hosted VPC.
- No transitive routing; use peering for single-tenant quick integrations.

3) VPN + Failover to Interconnect (Hybrid)
- Primary: Direct Interconnect to transit. Secondary: IPSec VPN over internet with automated health checks and BGP failover.
- Use pre-shared keys rotated by KMS or HSM integration.

Topology selection checklist
- Required throughput and 95th percentile sustained bandwidth. (If >5 Gbps sustained, prefer Direct Interconnect.)
- Regulatory/data residency requirements (if traffic must remain in-customer network, require private physical cross-connect).
- Latency SLOs (target RTT and jitter).
- Planned burst patterns and traffic shaping expectations.

Routing, BGP, and Filtering guidelines
- Use eBGP for interconnects; establish MD5 or TTL protections as supported.
- Advertise only the minimal set of prefixes. Use prefix-lists and AS-path filters.
- Set BGP community tags for route propagation and cost-based preference.
- Default route handling: do NOT advertise 0.0.0.0/0 from customer to Redwood control plane.
- Prefer route leak prevention at the transit gateway: explicit export maps required.

IP addressing and MTU
- Use /24 or larger subnets per AZ for control-plane endpoints to simplify filtering.
- Standard MTU: 1500 for public VPC subnets; 9001 (jumbo) where both sides support it for bulk KV/cache replication and large model artifacts (recommended for interconnects).
- Always validate Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) in acceptance tests.

Security controls and encryption
- Interconnect layer: enforce physical port isolation and VLAN segregation.
- BGP authentication (where supported) and strict community/AS checks.
- Transit encryption: if required by policy, terminate TLS between control-plane components and use end-to-end IPSec tunnels for data-plane paths.
- Key management: integrate with customer KMS/HSM for PSK rotation and TLS certs where requested.
- RBAC: limit who can create peering or route propagation changes. All changes require approval and an automated rollback window.

Provisioning and Terraform snippets
- Provide a minimal Terraform example for AWS Direct Connect + Transit Gateway attachment: (example is illustrative; adapt to account IDs and region)

terraform provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }
resource "aws_dx_connection" "customer_connection" { name = "redwood-cx" bandwidth = "1Gbps" }
resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway" "rtg" { description = "redwood-transit" }
resource "aws_dx_gateway" "dg" { name = "redwood-dxg" amazon_side_asn = 64512 }
resource "aws_dx_gateway_association" "dx_to_tgw" { dx_gateway_id = aws_dx_gateway.dg.id transit_gateway_id = aws_ec2_transit_gateway.rtg.id }
(Replace with provider-specific resources for GCP / Azure; validate local address families and VLAN tags.)

Acceptance tests (automated suite)
- Pre-provisioning validation: verify ASN, VLAN IDs, and advertised tenant prefixes with carrier.
- Connectivity test: establish BGP; verify neighbor state=Established.
  - Command examples:
    - AWS: aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments / aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-peering-attachments
    - On-prem router: show ip bgp summary | grep <remote-as>
- Latency and bandwidth: run iperf3 across peering path at 1m, 95th percentile and 99th percentile windows.
- PMTUD and fragmentation: send varied MTU packets (e.g., ping -M do -s) to validate.
- Route validation: check that only authorized prefixes are present and that no default route leakage exists.
- Encryption validation: validate IPSec SA and TLS ciphers; check cert chain in control-plane TLS endpoints.

Telemetry and observability
- Required metrics to be exported to Redwood monitoring stack and optionally to customer:
  - BGP session state (up/down, flaps)
  - Transit interface RX/TX, drop counts, errors
  - Flow logs for peered VPCs (sampled 1:1000 for billing, increase when debugging)
  - PMTU / ICMP fragmentation counters
- Standard tags: customer_id, deployment_id, region, interconnect_id
- Log retention: 90 days standard; 365 days on request (contracted).

Day-2 runbook: failover and rollback
- Scenario A: Direct interconnect flap
  1) Detect: BGP down alert triggers page and runbook.
  2) Validate: confirm carrier status via carrier portal and transit-cloud console.
  3) Action: if secondary VPN exists and is healthy, promote VPN routes by adjusting route priority (BGP MED/local-preference) and announce via automation.
  4) Notify: post status to customer Slack channel and update incident.
  5) Revert: after carrier confirms fix, withdraw temporary MED and re-enable original route advertisement.

- Scenario B: Route leak detected (unauthorized prefix)
  1) Isolate: immediately advertise more specific null-route (OR community-based blackhole) in transit gateway export map to prevent traffic blackholing other customers.
  2) Audit: collect RIB snapshots from both sides, export flow logs for the offending prefix, escalate to network security and carrier.
  3) Rollback: remove offending advertisement and restore export maps.

Maintenance and upgrade considerations
- Scheduled maintenance must have a 48h notice and a rollback window of at least 2 hours.
- Upgrade steps for transit gateway or cloud router:
  1) Verify control-plane replicas in passive AZ are fully synced and healthy.
  2) Drain existing BGP sessions to a maintenance route target using graceful restart where supported.
  3) Apply software/route-table changes in a canary region (single AZ) and run acceptance tests.
  4) Progressive rollout: 10% of attachments -> 30% -> 100% with automated health gating.
  5) On failure, execute the rollback automation to restore previous route maps and neighbor sessions.

Rollback automation primitives (required for all enterprise deployments)
- Snapshot current route tables and BGP RIB (timestamped JSON) to the configured telemetry bucket.
- Keep IaC and state versioned; use terraform state-locking and store state in a read-only snapshot for rollback agent.
- Run a pre-canned revert plan that: restores prior transit attachments, re-applies prefix-lists, and flips local-preference flags back.

Customer requirements matrix (minimums)
| Requirement | Minimum | Recommended | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Interconnect bandwidth | 500 Mbps | 1 Gbps | For model artifact pulls and KV sync, choose >=1 Gbps for low RTOs |
| ASN | customer-owned ASN or shared with consent | customer-owned ASN | Avoid overlapping private ASNs; use RFC1918-safe planning |
| MTU | 1500 | 9001 (jumbo) | Jumbo recommended for cluster replication traffic |
| BGP session redundancy | 1 | 2+ | Two sessions across diverse edges is required for SLA tier-2 |
| Monitoring export | Flow logs + BGP metrics | Add SNMP and sFlow on request | Agree on retention and access in contract |
(continued)
On‑site vs remote troubleshooting checklist
- On-site: physical cross-connect light check, VLAN tag inspection, patch panel labeling, fiber tester (OTDR) if available.
- Remote: collect BGP RIB, netstat summaries, iperf3 logs, traceroutes with timestamped hops, route table snapshots, flow logs.

Escalation contacts and SLAs
- First responder: Platform NetOps (page escalation) -> 15 minutes response target.
- Engineering escalation: Network SRE -> 1 hour.
- Carrier escalation: use carrier-defined escalation path; have account manager contact in contract.
- SLA targets to include in deployment contract:
  - Interconnect availability: 99.95% (higher tiers negotiable)
  - BGP stability (no flaps >3 per hour) for production routes
  - Mean time to restore (MTTR) for single-edge failure: 30 minutes (with VPN failover)

Appendices
A. Useful commands and checks
- Linux: ip route show; ip -s link; sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n "tcp port 179"
- Router: show ip bgp summary; show bgp neighbors; show interfaces counters
- PMTUD test: ping -M do -s 8972 <remote-ip>
- Bandwidth test: iperf3 -c <remote> -P 8 -t 60

B. Example incident severity decision table
- Sev1: complete control-plane isolation for >5% of customer traffic for >15 minutes.
- Sev2: local edge flaps or steady packet loss >1% affecting <5% traffic.
- Sev3: degraded but stable performance or single route leak isolated to non-critical prefixes.

C. Change request template (must be filled for any interconnect or peering change)
- Change title, owner, start time, duration, rollback plan, verification steps, notification list, impacted prefixes, test commands.
